subject: chemistry_ib
source: Podstawa programowa kształcenia ogólnego dla liceum ogólnokształcącego i technikum, chemia, zakres podstawowy (Dz.U. 2018 poz. 467, zm. Dz.U. 2024 poz. 996), działy I-V, VII, X, XII; uzupełnienia z IB DP Chemistry guide (first assessment 2025); zakres klasy 1 wg typowego rozkładu materiału

items.question: What does the atomic number (Z) of an element tell you?
accept: number of protons in the nucleus
items.explanation: Z is the number of protons in the nucleus; in a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.

items.question: What does the mass number (A) of an atom represent?
items.explanation: A = Z + N, the total number of nucleons in the nucleus.

items.question: How many neutrons are there in an atom of chlorine-37 (Z = 17)?
items.explanation: Neutrons = A - Z = 37 - 17 = 20.

items.text: Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of {{neutrons}} are called isotopes.
items.explanation: Isotopes such as C-12 and C-14 have the same number of protons but different mass numbers.

items.question: Which subatomic particle has a relative charge of -1 and a negligible mass?
items.explanation: Electrons occupy the space around the nucleus; their mass is about 1/1840 of a proton.

items.question: Which two subatomic particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
items.explanation: The nucleus contains almost all of the atom's mass; electrons move around it.

items.text: The relative atomic mass of an element is the weighted average mass of its {{isotopes}} compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
items.hint: atoms of the same element with different masses
items.explanation: This is why relative atomic masses in the periodic table are often not whole numbers.

items.question: Chlorine is 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37. What is its relative atomic mass?
What is the charge of the ion formed when a magnesium atom loses two electrons?
items.explanation: Losing electrons leaves an excess of protons, so the ion is a cation: Mg2+.

items.question: Write the full electron configuration of a sodium atom (Z = 11).
items.explanation: Eleven electrons fill the subshells in order of increasing energy: 2 + 2 + 6 + 1.

items.question: What is the maximum number of electrons that a p subshell can hold?
items.explanation: A p subshell has three orbitals, each holding at most two electrons.

items.question: What is the maximum number of electrons in the third shell (n = 3)?
items.explanation: The third shell has 3s, 3p and 3d subshells: 2 + 6 + 10 = 18 electrons (2n^2).

items.text: The condensed (shorthand) electron configuration of chlorine is [Ne] 3s2 {{3p5}}.
items.explanation: The noble-gas core [Ne] stands for 1s2 2s2 2p6; the remaining 7 electrons are 3s2 3p5.

items.question: Write the electron configuration of the chloride ion, Cl-.
items.explanation: Cl has 17 electrons; gaining one gives 18, the same configuration as argon.

items.question: According to the Aufbau principle, which subshell is filled after 3p?
items.explanation: The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so potassium is [Ar] 4s1.

items.question: How many unpaired electrons does a nitrogen atom (1s2 2s2 2p3) have?
items.explanation: By Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins.

items.question: Which principle states that an orbital can hold at most two electrons, with opposite spins?
items.explanation: Together with the Aufbau principle and Hund's rule it determines electron configurations.

items.question: What is a vertical column of the periodic table called?
items.explanation: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties.

items.question: What is a horizontal row of the periodic table called?
items.explanation: Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied electron shells.

items.question: To which block of the periodic table does sodium ([Ne] 3s1) belong?
items.explanation: The highest-energy electron is in an s subshell; groups 1 and 2 (and He) form the s block.

items.question: What does the period number of an element tell you about its atoms?
items.explanation: Sodium is in period 3, so its electrons occupy three shells.

items.question: For main-group elements, what does the group number (1, 2, 13-18) tell you?
items.explanation: Group 1 has 1 valence electron, group 17 has 7 (group number minus 10).

items.text: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius {{decreases}} because nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell.
items.hint: the nucleus pulls the electrons closer
items.explanation: Shielding stays almost constant, so the effective nuclear charge rises.

items.text: Down a group, atomic radius {{increases}} because each new period adds another electron shell.
items.explanation: The extra inner shells also shield the outer electrons from the nucleus.

items.question: How does the first ionisation energy change across a period from left to right?
items.explanation: Greater nuclear charge and smaller radius make it harder to remove an electron.

items.question: Which element in period 3 has the largest atomic radius?
items.explanation: Radius decreases across a period, so the first element, sodium, is the largest.

items.question: What is the name of the group 1 metals?
items.explanation: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs are soft, reactive metals that form alkaline hydroxides with water.

items.question: What is the name of the group 17 elements?
items.explanation: F, Cl, Br, I are reactive non-metals that form halide ions (X-).

items.question: Which group contains the very unreactive gases helium, neon and argon?
items.explanation: Noble gases have full outer shells, so they rarely form compounds.

items.text: Down group 1, the reactivity of the alkali metals {{increases}} because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily.
items.hint: potassium reacts more violently with water than sodium
items.explanation: Lower ionisation energy means the metal is oxidised more readily.

items.question: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
items.explanation: Fluorine has a Pauling electronegativity of 4.0, the highest of all elements.

items.text: Across a period electronegativity {{increases}}, and down a group it decreases.
items.hint: fluorine is the most electronegative element
items.explanation: Small atoms with high nuclear charge attract bonding electrons most strongly.

items.question: What type of bonding forms between a metal and a non-metal by transfer of electrons?
items.explanation: The metal forms a cation and the non-metal an anion; the ions attract electrostatically.

items.question: What type of bond is formed when two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons?
items.explanation: Each shared pair counts towards the full outer shell of both atoms.

items.question: What type of bonding is present in a piece of copper?
items.explanation: Metal cations are held in a lattice by a sea of delocalised electrons.

items.question: Using Pauling electronegativities, what kind of covalent bond forms when the difference is zero, as in Cl-Cl?
items.explanation: Equal electronegativities mean the electron pair is shared equally.

items.question: The electronegativity difference between H (2.2) and Cl (3.2) is 1.0. What type of bond is H-Cl?
items.explanation: The shared pair is pulled towards chlorine, giving a dipole with H delta+ and Cl delta-.

items.question: Which ions are present in sodium chloride, NaCl?
items.explanation: Sodium loses one electron and chlorine gains one, giving ions with full outer shells.

items.question: How many lone pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom in a water molecule have?
items.explanation: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons: 2 are used in the two O-H bonds and 4 form two lone pairs.

items.question: How many bonding pairs of electrons are shared in a nitrogen molecule, N2?
items.explanation: N2 has a triple bond; each nitrogen atom also keeps one lone pair.

items.text: A single covalent bond is always a {{sigma}} bond, formed by head-on overlap of orbitals.
items.explanation: Pi bonds form by sideways overlap of p orbitals and occur only in double and triple bonds.

items.question: A double bond consists of one sigma bond and how many pi bonds?
items.explanation: A triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds.

items.text: CO2 has polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is non-polar because its {{linear}} shape makes the bond dipoles cancel.
items.explanation: Water is bent, so its dipoles do not cancel and H2O is polar.

items.question: Which type of crystal is hard, brittle, has a high melting point and conducts electricity only when molten or dissolved?
items.explanation: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice; they move only in the melt or in solution.

items.question: Which type of crystal consists of molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces and has a low melting point, e.g. iodine?
items.explanation: Only the weak forces between molecules need to be overcome, not covalent bonds.

items.text: Metals conduct electricity because their {{delocalised}} electrons are free to move through the lattice of cations.
items.explanation: The same mobile electrons make metals good conductors of heat and give them lustre.

items.question: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon. What is this phenomenon called?
items.explanation: Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.

items.question: Which allotrope of carbon conducts electricity because each carbon atom contributes one delocalised electron?
items.explanation: In graphite each carbon is bonded to three others; the fourth electron is delocalised over the layer.

items.question: Name the allotrope of carbon that is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons.
items.explanation: Graphene is one layer of graphite: extremely strong, thin and a good conductor.

items.text: Diamond is extremely hard because each carbon atom is covalently bonded to {{four}} others in a giant covalent (network) lattice.
items.hint: number of bonds per carbon atom
items.explanation: Breaking the crystal would require breaking many strong covalent bonds.

items.question: Name the carbon allotrope that forms hollow spheres of 60 carbon atoms (C60).
items.explanation: Fullerenes are molecular, so unlike diamond and graphite they dissolve in some organic solvents.

items.question: What is the strongest type of intermolecular force?
items.explanation: Hydrogen bonds are still much weaker than covalent or ionic bonds.

items.question: Which intermolecular force exists between all molecules, including non-polar ones such as CH4?
items.explanation: Temporary dipoles arise from the random movement of electrons.

items.text: Hydrogen bonding occurs when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to N, O or {{F/fluorine}} and attracted to a lone pair on another such atom.
items.explanation: H-Cl does not form hydrogen bonds because chlorine is less electronegative and larger.

items.question: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide, H2S?
items.explanation: Water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds; H2S molecules do not.

items.text: The boiling points of alkanes increase with chain length because London dispersion forces become {{stronger}} as the number of electrons increases.
items.explanation: Methane is a gas, octane a liquid and C20 alkanes are waxy solids.

items.question: What is the value of the Avogadro constant?
items.explanation: One mole contains 6.02 x 10^23 elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions).

items.question: What is the SI unit of amount of substance?
items.explanation: One mole is the amount containing as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12.

items.text: The number of particles in one mole of substance is called the {{Avogadro}} constant.
items.explanation: Its symbol is NA (or L); N = n x NA.

items.question: Which formula links amount of substance (n), mass (m) and molar mass (M)?
items.explanation: Rearranged: m = n x M and M = m / n.

items.question: Calculate the molar mass of water, H2O (H = 1.0, O = 16.0).
Calculate the molar mass of carbon dioxide, CO2 (C = 12.0, O = 16.0).
How many moles of water are there in 9.0 g of H2O (M = 18.0 g/mol)?
What is the mass of 2.0 mol of sodium chloride, NaCl (M = 58.5 g/mol)?
What is the molar volume of any gas under normal conditions (0 °C, 1013 hPa)?
items.explanation: At 0 °C and 1013 hPa one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm3.

items.question: What molar volume of a gas does the IB use at STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa)?
items.explanation: IB STP is 100 kPa, slightly lower pressure than 1013 hPa, so the volume is slightly larger than 22.4 dm3.

items.question: What volume does 0.5 mol of oxygen gas occupy under normal conditions (molar volume 22.4 dm3/mol)?

items.text: According to Avogadro's law, equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of {{molecules/particles/moles}}.
items.hint: what the volume of a gas depends on
items.explanation: This is why gas volumes in an equation can be read in the same ratio as the mole coefficients.

items.question: Balance the equation: H2 + O2 -> H2O. Give the coefficients in order.
items.explanation: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O: four H and two O atoms on each side.

items.question: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many moles of water form from 3 mol of H2 with excess oxygen?
items.explanation: The mole ratio H2 : H2O is 2 : 2 = 1 : 1.

items.question: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many moles of O2 are needed to react completely with 4 mol of H2?
items.explanation: The mole ratio H2 : O2 is 2 : 1, so 4 mol H2 needs 2 mol O2.

items.question: What mass of CO2 forms when 12 g of carbon burns completely (C + O2 -> CO2; M(CO2) = 44 g/mol)?
items.explanation: 12 g of carbon is 1 mol, which gives 1 mol of CO2 = 44 g.

items.text: In a chemical reaction the total mass of the products {{equals}} the total mass of the reactants (law of conservation of mass).
items.hint: atoms are neither created nor destroyed
items.explanation: This is why equations must be balanced: the same atoms appear on both sides.

items.text: The {{empirical}} formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
items.hint: the other kind is the molecular formula
items.explanation: For glucose C6H12O6 the empirical formula is CH2O.

items.question: What is the empirical formula of glucose, C6H12O6?
items.explanation: Divide all subscripts by the highest common factor, 6.

items.question: A compound has the empirical formula CH2 and a molar mass of 56 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?
items.explanation: M(CH2) = 14; 56 / 14 = 4, so the molecular formula is (CH2)4 = C4H8.

items.question: A hydrocarbon contains 75% carbon and 25% hydrogen by mass (C = 12, H = 1). What is its empirical formula?
In a reaction, which reactant is completely used up first and so determines the maximum amount of product?
items.explanation: The other reactant is in excess and some of it remains after the reaction.

items.question: The theoretical yield of a reaction is 10.0 g and the actual yield is 8.0 g. What is the percentage yield?

items.text: Percentage yield = {{actual}} yield / theoretical yield x 100%.
items.explanation: Yields are below 100% because of side reactions, incomplete reactions and losses during purification.

items.question: Which formula gives the molar concentration of a solution?
items.explanation: n in mol, V in dm3, so c is in mol/dm3.

items.question: What is the molar concentration when 0.5 mol of NaCl is dissolved to make 2.0 dm3 of solution?
What mass of solute is in 200 g of a 5% (by mass) solution?
items.explanation: m(solute) = 5% x 200 g = 10 g.

items.question: What is the percentage concentration (by mass) when 20 g of salt is dissolved in 80 g of water?
items.explanation: Cp = 20 g / (20 g + 80 g) x 100% = 20%; the solution mass includes the solute.

items.text: {{Solubility}} is the maximum mass of a substance that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature to give a saturated solution.
items.explanation: For most solids solubility increases with temperature; for gases it decreases.

items.text: Adding more solvent to a solution is called {{dilution}}; the amount of solute stays the same but the concentration falls.
items.explanation: Useful relation: c1 x V1 = c2 x V2.

items.question: A solution of salt in water is clear with no visible particles. Is it homogeneous or heterogeneous?
items.explanation: A true solution is a homogeneous mixture: its composition is uniform throughout.

items.question: What is a mixture of two immiscible liquids in which tiny droplets of one are dispersed in the other (e.g. milk, mayonnaise)?
items.explanation: Emulsions are heterogeneous; emulsifiers such as lecithin stabilise them.

items.question: Which technique separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper?
items.explanation: The liquid that passes through is the filtrate; the solid left behind is the residue.

items.question: Which technique separates two miscible liquids with different boiling points, e.g. ethanol and water?
items.explanation: The liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates first and is condensed.

items.question: Which technique separates substances by how far they travel in a solvent across paper or a thin layer?
items.explanation: Components with greater affinity for the solvent travel further.

items.question: Which technique transfers a solute from one liquid into a second, immiscible solvent in which it is more soluble?
items.explanation: It is carried out in a separating funnel, e.g. removing iodine from water with hexane.

items.question: What do we call a reaction that releases energy to the surroundings as heat?
items.explanation: Combustion and neutralisation are exothermic; the temperature of the surroundings rises.

items.question: What do we call a reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, so the products have more energy than the reactants?
items.explanation: Thermal decomposition of CaCO3 and photosynthesis are endothermic.

items.question: What is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react?
items.explanation: On an energy profile diagram it is the height of the barrier between reactants and the transition state.

items.question: What is the sign of the enthalpy change, delta H, for an exothermic reaction?
items.explanation: Energy leaves the system, so the enthalpy of the products is lower than that of the reactants.

items.question: What is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up?
items.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts; catalytic converters in cars use platinum.

items.text: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a {{lower}} activation energy.
items.hint: the barrier changes, delta H does not
items.explanation: More collisions have enough energy to react; the enthalpy change stays the same.

items.question: The rate of a reaction is defined as the change in what quantity per unit time?
items.explanation: Rate = change in concentration / time, typically in mol/(dm3 s).

items.question: How does grinding a solid reactant into a powder affect the rate of reaction?
items.explanation: A larger surface area means more particles are exposed and collisions are more frequent.

items.text: Raising the temperature increases the rate of reaction because more particles have energy greater than or equal to the {{activation}} energy and collisions are more frequent.
items.explanation: Rate roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in many reactions.

items.question: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO is an example of which type of reaction?
items.explanation: Two substances combine to form one product; it is also a combustion (and redox) reaction.

items.question: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 is an example of which type of reaction?
items.explanation: One compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances on heating.

items.question: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
items.explanation: Methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8: each has two more hydrogens than twice the carbons.

items.question: What is a series of compounds with the same functional group in which each member differs from the next by CH2?
items.explanation: Members show a gradual change in physical properties and similar chemical properties.

items.question: Which functional group, -OH, is characteristic of alcohols?
items.explanation: Ethanol, C2H5OH, is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks.

items.question: Compounds containing the -COOH group belong to which class?
items.explanation: Ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH3COOH, is the acid in vinegar.

items.question: Which hydrocarbons contain at least one C=C double bond?
items.explanation: Alkenes are unsaturated; their general formula is CnH2n.

items.question: Which piece of glassware is used to prepare a solution of an exact volume, e.g. 250.0 cm3?
items.explanation: The solute is dissolved, then solvent is added up to the calibration mark.

items.question: Which piece of equipment delivers precise, variable volumes of liquid in a titration?
items.explanation: A pipette delivers one fixed volume; a burette is read before and after to find the volume added.

items.question: What must you wear to protect your eyes whenever chemicals are used in the lab?
items.explanation: Eye protection is worn throughout the experiment, not only when pouring.

items.question: What does a hazard pictogram showing a flame mean?
items.explanation: Flammable substances such as ethanol are kept away from open flames.

items.question: What does a hazard pictogram showing a skull and crossbones mean?
items.explanation: The pictogram with a test tube dripping on a hand and a bar means corrosive.

items.question: When diluting concentrated sulfuric acid, which liquid do you add to which?
accept: pour the acid into the water
items.explanation: The dilution is strongly exothermic; adding water to acid can make it boil and spit.

items.question: Which piece of glassware delivers one fixed, accurate volume of liquid, e.g. 25.00 cm3?
items.explanation: A pipette filler is used to draw up the liquid; never pipette by mouth.
